title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
Udio, an AI music generation service, trained its models on recorded music without first securing licenses from the rights holders. This is a case of a system built and deployed using data that the data's owners allege was taken without permission or compensation. The failure occurred at the training stage, before the product reached users, meaning any output the system generated carried the legal exposure embedded in how it was built.

Universal Music Group settled its claims against Udio and reached a licensing agreement under which a future platform will be trained only on authorized music. Warner Music Group did the same. Sony Music filed a separate new lawsuit alleging Udio copied more than 30,000 recordings, a claim that arose after a court barred Sony from adding those titles to its original case. A class action brought by independent artists was allowed to proceed, though the court moved it to a different jurisdiction. A musicians' union also filed suit, and UMG separately sought to have that union's claims dismissed.

None of the lawsuits beyond the UMG and WMG matters have produced a final verdict, and the allegations in the Sony case and the class action are not established findings. What the settlements do confirm is that deploying a generative model trained on commercially released recordings, without licenses in place, created legal liability that the company then had to resolve through negotiation rather than any technical fix applied after the fact.

summary:
Universal Music Group has settled its lawsuit against AI music startup Udio, reaching licensing agreements that resolve allegations that Udio used copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence model. The dispute centered on whether Udio improperly used hits like The Temptations' "My Girl" to generate similar melodies without permission or compensation. Under the settlement, Udio will launch a new platform next year trained exclusively on authorized and licensed music, allowing users to customize, stream and share their creations.

The agreement marks Udio's first major licensing deal with a major record label. Udio's CEO stated the partnership demonstrates how AI can empower artists and fans while fairly compensating creators who opt into the platform. Financial terms were not disclosed. Udio, founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees, has attracted millions of users since launching. UMG also announced a separate partnership with Stability AI on Thursday to develop music creation tools for artists and producers, further expanding the label's collaboration with artificial intelligence companies.
